title: “The Skeptic”: Prelude and Fugue No.6, Book I
content_blocks: Forgive me—my description of this prelude and fugue gets technical.  I’ll try to temper that in later posts!

This prelude and fugue uses a 22 note mode covering six octaves.  In the center, the notes are close together, but they spread out at the very top and bottom.  This means that going from one note on the scale to the next at the extremes of the piano cover a much wider range than going from one note to the next in the middle.  It is like city blocks:  going three blocks west from York Avenue to 3rd Avenue in the Upper East Side of Manhattan is more than 3 times longer than going three blocks west from Essex Avenue to Allen Street in the Lower East Side.

The prelude starts near the middle of that scale, swaying from one pitch to another.  As the swaying expands, the steps take more and more space.  Eventually this leads to the heart of the prelude, in which a pair of overlapping descending and ascending lines expand and contract.  In the same way, the time between the start of the descending line and the start of the ascending line contracts from 5 beats, to 3, and finally to 1 beat, changing where the lines cross.  The lines are also shadowed by note a sixth above or below them, creating a beautiful aura.

This fugue subject is probably the most Bach-like of my fugues, perhaps recalling Bach’s Art of the Fugue. My fugue features “diatonic answers” (see the next mini-blog “explainer” post!) and also many different stretti (the narrowing or “hurrying up” of the timing of the entrance of the answer relative to the subject), various compressions and decompressions of the pace of the subject entries, as well as inversions of the subject.

As I was finishing Book I, it occurred to me that it might be fun to give each piece a character name, similar to the way Couperin gives many of the pieces in his Pièces de Clavecin character names—some curious and obscure, some obvious. Since I was adding those names after completing the compositions (unlike what I did with Book II)—I felt that those names were too artificial, and I left them off the published version. It’s been at least four years since I thought about those names. Revisiting them now, some of them seem exactly right, while others seem obscure even to me. I will include those character names in these blog posts—you can let me know what you think! The name for this pair of pieces was “The Skeptic.”
You can listen to Mika Sasaki’s performance of the Prelude and Fugue on YouTube.
